narrative: Your application was denied because the model estimated a 68.9% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That means, based on the information available, failure was considered more likely than passing; it is a risk estimate, not a certainty. The decision was driven mainly by your academic standing in law school. Your third-year class standing was the single most influential factor and pushed the prediction toward failure; your first-year standing was the next strongest factor and also pushed toward failure. Both placed you in the second decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile, so this was a substantial difference from the typical admitted profile. Your undergraduate GPA, at 3.0 versus an accepted-student average of 3.23, was the third most influential factor, but among these top factors it was the one that pushed toward passing rather than failing. To improve a future application, focus on strengthening your academic record, especially upper-level performance, and seek advising from admissions and bar-readiness staff. Consider additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate program, retake the LSAT if your score can be improved, and apply to schools that review applications holistically. Provide context for any circumstances affecting your grades, and ask advisors how to demonstrate readiness for bar study.
